Chapter 7: Overcoming Resistance and Building Buy-In
Even when you’ve got a solid framework in place, real change almost always bumps into resistance. People might worry that new ways of working will disrupt what they’re used to, put their jobs at risk, or even highlight mistakes they've made in the past. If you want improvements to stick, these are the concerns you’ve got to tackle head-on.
So, how do you do it? One of the best moves is to get everyone involved right from the start—and keep them in the loop as things evolve. When your team helps spot the roadblocks and dream up solutions, they’re way more likely to back the changes. Suddenly, improvements aren’t something done to them—they’re something done with them.
Trust plays a huge role in this. Leaders who share information openly—who explain, for example, how lowering inventory can free up cash for raises or cool new equipment—help everyone see the bigger picture. And don’t underestimate the power of a good story. Sharing real-world examples, like how small tweaks led to big wins in another team or company, makes change feel much more doable.
Of course, change can be uncomfortable. It’s totally normal to feel uneasy or even mess up a little along the way. What really matters is creating a safe space where people can experiment, take risks, and even fail—because that’s how you spark innovation and real learning.
Let’s talk about some practical ways to build buy-in:
First, try regular team huddles—quick daily check-ins where everyone can talk about progress or voice concerns.
Next, make your metrics visible. Post things like throughput, inventory, and operating expenses where everyone can see them.
Recognition goes a long way, too. Celebrate individuals and teams, no matter how small the win.
And don’t forget feedback loops. Encourage suggestions, and act on them fast so people know their voices matter.
When you focus on open communication, participation, and recognizing contributions, resistance starts to fade. Over time, you’ll notice the culture shifting—from just following orders, to a real sense of shared ownership and pride in making things better.
